issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants-accused under sections 201, 300, 302, IPC read with section 34, based on circumstantial evidence (consisting of evidence of last seen, extra judicial confession, recovery of weapon of offence and motive), is justified.

facts: The appellants were convicted for murder and destruction of evidence (sections 201, 300, 302, IPC read with section 34) by the trial court, and this conviction was confirmed by the High Court.

The conviction was based entirely on circumstantial evidence, which the prosecution argued consisted of four links: the 'last seen' theory, an extra-judicial confession, the recovery of the weapon of offence, and motive.
The prosecution had initially charged the appellants with kidnapping for murder (Section 364 IPC) but failed to produce any evidence for this charge and effectively abandoned it during the trial.
law: For a conviction to be based on circumstantial evidence, the chain of evidence must be complete and unerringly point to the guilt of the accused, excluding any other hypothesis.

The 'last seen' theory, as a link in circumstantial evidence, requires the oral testimony of at least one witness who can establish that the deceased was last seen alive in the company of the accused.
Applying the 'last seen' theory without any positive evidence to support it is considered hazardous and impermissible.
application: The Supreme Court found a critical failure in the prosecution's case regarding the 'last seen' evidence.
It noted the "categoric finding" of the lower courts that not a single prosecution witness had testified to seeing the deceased alive in the company of the accused.

Despite this lack of evidence, the trial court and High Court had presumed the presence of the deceased with the appellants, which the Supreme Court deemed an "utterly perverse" appreciation of evidence.
The Court concluded that the 'last seen' link in the chain of circumstantial evidence was completely missing.
It further held that the other links in the chain (confession, recovery, motive), whether considered individually or collectively, were insufficient to connect the appellants to the crime.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction because the chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and broken. The most crucial link, the 'last seen' evidence, was found to be non-existent as no witness could place the deceased with the accused. Since the evidence, even when taken collectively, was insufficient to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, the Court set aside the lower courts' judgments and acquitted the appellants, granting them the benefit of the doubt.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In criminal cases, the prosecution is required to establish its case as it was put forth; if the court disbelieves any aspect of that case, the court cannot create a new case on its own for the prosecution, as there is no room for conjectures and surmises.
obiter: There is a distinction between proving the factum of a statement made by other persons and proving the truth of such a statement.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Having carefully considered the rival contentions and perusing the evidence on record, which made us to make the observations, conclusions and ﬁ ndings as above, we have no hesitation to hold that the trial Court as also the High Court have appreciated the evidence in an utterly perverse manner viz., against the weight of evidence.
legal_tests_applied: When the prosecution comes out with a motive and the motive is either not proved or held to be insuﬃ cient, the evidence of witnesses of the said fact has to be scrutinized with great care and caution.
the burden to prove the prosecution case in criminal matters involving oﬀ ences in respect of which the appellants were made to stand the trial, is on the prosecution.

If the prosecution got no good reason for not producing the best evidence, in the sense, the best witness who could help the prosecution to establish their case, then adverse inference could have been taken only against the prosecution and certainly that cannot be a reason to hold that the defence could have distorted/ disproved the motive that was projected by the prosecution by examining that witness.
